title: Required flags are unmarked in usage and inexpressible in the manifest (lore impact --direction, and four more)
description:
Usage is 'lore impact <id>' and the flag list does not identify --direction as required. 'lore impact PGF-3 --kind task --json' exits 2 with '--direction is required'. Adding --direction outbound succeeds, and the documented example does carry one -- so the requirement exists and is correct, it's just invisible until the command fails.

Help usability, not a graph correctness bug -- but the machine-manifest half matters more than it looks, since that is what an agent reads to construct a valid invocation without trial-and-error.

Fix: show the requirement in usage, and expose required flags in the machine manifest (lore's --json manifest / help output), or give --direction a documented default.

Source: 2026-09-13 proof-graph inspection (Lore 0.6.0, Quest 0.6.0), read-only against production, recorded as OPAG-120 on opum-agent.

acceptanceCriteria.text: `lore help impact` distinguishes its REQUIRED flags (`--kind`, `--direction`) from its optional ones, and `lore help path` does the same for `--from-kind`, `--to-kind` and `--direction` -- all five, not only the one that was reported.

`lore manifest --json` expresses requiredness machine-readably, so an agent enumerating the contract can tell a mandatory flag from an optional one. The field is ADDITIVE, so a consumer that does not know it is unaffected -- the same property that made the LCLI-366 `kind` field safe.

A regression test ties the manifest's required markers to the ACTUAL parser, so a flag that becomes required, or stops being, cannot silently drift from what the manifest claims. Verified mutation-sensitive: flip one marker and the test must fail.

Every command is audited for the same defect, not only the two reached by the reporter's tooling. Conditionally-required flags enforced by ad-hoc `throw usage(...)` -- `--force requires --out`, `--repository requires --workspace`, `--from`/`--to` together, `--workspace requires retained snapshot selectors` -- are either covered or EXPLICITLY ruled out of scope with a reason on this record.

If the `--direction`-gets-a-default alternative is taken instead, it is argued on the record against the three objections already raised (it resolves one flag of five, does nothing for `lore path`, and leaves the manifest still unable to express requiredness for anything) -- not chosen by default.
If the manifest carries a schema version this change affects, it is bumped and its contract test updated; if it does not, that is stated rather than left implicit.
`bun run lint`, `typecheck` and the test suite pass, and `lore check` exits 0.

implementationNotes:
WIDENED 2026-09-14 after mbpm2 RE-REPORTED this against the published 0.6.2. It was already filed
here (from their 2026-09-13 proof-graph inspection of 0.6.0, OPAG-120), and a second session filed
it AGAIN as LCLI-493 before finding this record. LCLI-493 is archived as the duplicate; everything
it established is folded in below. The two facts it added are the reason this record is retitled and
re-scoped rather than merely annotated.

ONE INSTANCE WAS REPORTED. THERE ARE FIVE. Measured on dev at 661529cf, not inferred.
`requiredChoice` (src/commands/traversal.ts:29,45) governs:

    lore impact  --kind        --direction
    lore path    --from-kind   --to-kind    --direction

All five are mandatory. None is marked. `lore help impact` renders every flag in one
undifferentiated list, so `--direction` looks exactly as optional as `--limit`. Fixing only the
reported flag would leave four identical defects behind, and would leave `lore path` -- which needs
THREE of them -- completely unaddressed.

THE ROOT CAUSE IS IN THE CONTRACT, NOT THE RENDERER, and this is the half worth the most.
`ManifestFlag` (src/core/manifest.ts:52) carries `name`, `alias`, `takesValue`, `repeatable`,
`summary` and `kind` -- and NO WAY WHATSOEVER to express that a flag is required. So the help
renderer is not withholding information it has; it has none. Neither does anything reading
`lore manifest --json`.

That is what makes this more than a help-text nicety. The manifest exists so an agent can enumerate
what the CLI accepts WITHOUT reading its source. An agent doing that today is told `--direction` is
an ordinary optional flag, constructs `lore impact <id> --kind task`, and gets exit 2. The CLI is
machine-describing a command that does not exist. The contract was SILENT rather than wrong, and
silence parses as "optional".

SAME SHAPE AS LCLI-366, which is also where the fix shape comes from: a flag that terminates with
its own envelope (`--version`) was undeclared through 0.3.5, and was fixed by ADDING an optional
field to the manifest rather than restructuring it. An optional `required?: boolean` is additive in
exactly the same way -- a consumer that does not know the field is unaffected.

RESONANCE WITH QUEST, noted by the orchestrator and worth carrying into the 0.7.0 pair: quest moved
`data.task` to `data` while both shapes still reported `schemaVersion: 1`, so a consumer could not
select a decoder. Two sibling products, two machine-readable contracts, both silent about something
a consumer needed. The shared principle, if we adopt it for 0.7.0: ANYTHING AN AGENT PARSES MUST BE
ABLE TO EXPRESS WHAT IT DOES NOT CURRENTLY SAY.

AUDIT THE WHOLE SURFACE, NOT THE FIVE. Other commands enforce requirements through ad-hoc
`throw usage(...)` rather than `requiredChoice`, and several are CONDITIONAL, which a plain boolean
cannot express: `--force requires --out` (src/commands/agent.ts:428), `--repository requires
--workspace` (src/commands/args.ts:181), `--from and --to must be supplied together` and `--workspace
requires retained snapshot selectors` (src/commands/explorer.ts:169,172). Decide deliberately whether
they are in scope; if they are not, SAY SO on the record rather than leaving the next reader to
wonder why some mandatory flags are marked and others are not.

The original AC#3 offered "or --direction gets a documented default and the required-flag error is
removed" as an alternative. That alternative is now WEAK and should not be taken without argument:
it resolves one flag of five, does nothing for `lore path`, and leaves the manifest still unable to
say "required" for anything -- which is the defect an agent consumer actually hits. A default also
silently changes traversal semantics for anyone who omitted the flag expecting an error.
